facts.text: The statue was finished and unveiled in New York Harbor in 1886.
When it was completed in 1886, the statue was brown, like a new American penny, not green.
The statue's outer skin is copper about 3/32 inch (2.4 mm) thick, about as thick as two pennies placed together.
The statue's copper oxidized naturally and formed a green coating called a patina.
Copper metal oxidizes slowly when it is left in the open air for a long time, forming a blue-green coating made of various copper compounds.
Salt water and damp air in New York Harbor slowly changed the statue to turquoise green.
Black-and-white photographs suggest that the statue first looked brown or dark gray.
Because color photography did not exist yet, the exact timing of the color change is hard to know.
The National Park Service believes the change to green took about 25 to 30 years.
By 1906 the once-bright copper statue had a sea-green patina.
In many places the patina is as thick as the copper under it, and it protects the copper from wearing away.
Copper patinas usually take a long time to form, but a classroom demonstration can produce one on copper coins within tens of seconds.
The statue's inner frame is made of iron and stainless steel.
Restoration began in 1984 and was finished in 1986, in time for the statue's 100th birthday celebrated on July 4, 1986.
During the restoration, the rusting iron bars that joined the copper skin to the inner frame were replaced with stainless steel bars.
Workers repaired holes in the copper skin and removed layers of paint from the inside of the skin and from the inner iron frame.
The water-damaged torch was replaced with a copy of the original design, covered in gold; the old torch was removed in 1984 and is shown in a museum.
French and American architects, engineers and conservators planned the restoration together.

notes: 批次規格提示的「1906 年曾有人想把它漆掉」在白名單來源（nps.gov、loc.gov、smithsonianmag.com 等）讀不到可核對的原文（Smithsonian 頁面擋自動讀取，其他提到此事的是白名單外的網站），所以題目不寫這件事；具體事件改用 1886 年落成時是銅色、1906 年已是綠色，以及 1984–1986 年的修復。
